He thereupon bowed and went away. Saw no one in the street at that time. It is a side-street—exceedingly solitary.

“William Bird, tailor, deposes that he belonged to the party which entered the house. Is an Englishman. Has resided in Paris for two years. Was among the earliest to mount the stairs. Heard the disputing voices. The harsh voice belonged to a Frenchman. Distinguished several words, but cannot now recollect them all. Clearly heard ‘sacré’ and ‘mon Dieu.’ At that instant there was a noise resembling several people struggling—a scraping, shuffling sound. The piercing voice was exceedingly loud—louder than the harsh one. Is certain it was not an Englishman's voice. Seemed to belong to a German. It might have been a woman's. Does not comprehend German.

“Four of the witnesses already named, upon being recalled, testified that the door of the room where Mademoiselle L.'s body was discovered was locked within when the party arrived. All was wholly silent—neither groans nor sounds of any description. When the door was forced, nobody was visible. The windows of both the rear and front chambers were lowered and securely fastened inside. A door communicating between the rooms was shut, though unlocked. The door from the front chamber to the passage was locked, the key remaining within. A little room at the front of the house, on the fourth floor at the passage's end, stood open, its door ajar. It was filled with old bedsteads, boxes, and similar things. These were cautiously taken out and examined. No inch of any part of the house escaped a thorough search. Chimney-sweeps were sent both up and down the chimneys. The building had four stories, with garrets (mansardes). A trap-door in the roof was most firmly nailed shut—seemed not to have been opened in years. The witnesses gave different accounts of the interval between hearing the quarrelling voices and forcing the chamber door. Some estimated only three minutes—others as many as five. Considerable difficulty attended the opening of the door.

“Alfonzo Garcio, undertaker, deposes that his residence is in the Rue Morgue. Is Spanish by birth. Belonged to the party entering the house. Did not go upstairs. Is of a nervous disposition, and feared the effects of excitement. Heard the voices disputing. The rough voice belonged to a Frenchman. Could not make out the words spoken. The piercing voice belonged to an Englishman—of this he is certain.

While these events were taking place in the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in the old hideout—the very one from which the girl had taken Oliver—lost in thought before a smoky, low-burning fire. A pair of bellows rested on his knee. He had apparently been trying to make the fire burn more brightly, but his thoughts had drawn him away. With his arms folded over the bellows and his chin resting on his thumbs, he stared absently at the rusty grate.

Behind him, the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling sat at a table, absorbed in a game of whist. The Dodger played against Bates and Chitling, also playing the cards dealt to the empty fourth seat. His face, always unusually sharp and knowing, grew still more interesting as he studied the game and carefully inspected Mr. Chitling's cards. Whenever he had the chance, he gave his neighbour's hand a searching glance and wisely adjusted his own play to what he discovered there. The night was cold, so the Dodger kept his hat on, as he often did indoors anyway. He also held a clay pipe between his teeth. He took it out only briefly when he felt the need to drink from a quart pot on the table, which stood filled with gin and water for everyone to share.

Master Bates, too, paid attention to the game. But he was more excitable than his accomplished friend, and he drank from the pot more often. He also made many jokes and unrelated remarks, all most unsuitable for a serious match of whist. Indeed, relying on their close friendship, the Artful more than once spoke gravely to him about this improper behaviour. Master Bates accepted these lectures with excellent humour. He simply told his friend to be “blowed,” suggested he put his head in a sack, or answered with some equally polished joke. Mr. Chitling greatly admired the way these witty replies fitted the occasion. It was striking that Chitling and his partner always lost. Far from making Master Bates angry, this seemed to entertain him enormously. At the end of every hand he roared with laughter and declared he had never played such a jolly game in his life.

“That's two doubles and the match,” said Mr. Chitling, looking thoroughly miserable as he pulled half a crown from his waistcoat pocket. “I never saw anyone like you, Jack. You win everything.

“Only a tick.”

“Where did you find him?”

“Out in the woods.”

“What would you take for him?”

“I dunno. I ain't wanting to sell him.”

“All right, then. He's a mighty little tick, anyhow.”

“Oh, anybody can speak poorly of a tick that ain't theirs. I'm content with him. He's tick enough for me.”

“Sho, ticks are plentiful. I could get a thousand if I cared to.”

“Well, why ain't you? Becuz you know perfectly well you can't. I reckon this is a mighty early tick. It's the first I've seen this year.”

“Look here, Huck—I'll trade you my tooth for him.”

“Let's have a look.”

Tom produced a scrap of paper and unfolded it with care. Huckleberry gazed at the contents longingly. The temptation was powerful. Finally he asked:

“Is it the genuwyne thing?”

Tom raised his lip, displaying the empty place.

“Well, all right,” Huckleberry said, “we've got a bargain.”

Tom shut the tick inside the percussion-cap box which had so recently served as the pinchbug's jail, and the two boys parted, both feeling richer than they had before.

On reaching the small, solitary frame school-house, Tom marched smartly inside, with the air of having made all honest haste. He put his hat upon a peg and dropped into his seat with business-like promptness. Enthroned above them in his large splint-bottom arm-chair, the master was nodding, soothed by the sleepy murmur of study. This disturbance woke him.

“Thomas Sawyer!”

Tom understood that his name, when spoken in full, foretold trouble.

“Sir!”

“Come here. Now, sir, what makes you late again, as usual?”

Tom was just preparing to shelter behind a falsehood when he noticed two long braids of yellow hair falling over a back which love's electric sympathy enabled him to recognize. Beside that figure lay the one empty seat on the girls' side of the room. Immediately he answered:

“I stopped to speak with Huckleberry Finn!”

The master's pulse halted, and he stared in helpless astonishment. The drone of study stopped. The scholars wondered whether this reckless boy had gone mad. The master asked:

“You—you did what?”

“Stopped to speak with Huckleberry Finn.”

The words admitted of no mistake.

“Thomas Sawyer, that is the most extraordinary confession I ever heard. A mere ferule is insufficient for such an offence. Remove your jacket.”

The master's arm laboured until it grew weary and the supply of switches had considerably shrunk. Then came the command:

“Now, sir, sit over there with the girls! And take warning from this.”

The ripple of tittering through the room seemed to shame the boy; in truth, however, his confusion sprang more from reverent awe of his unknown idol and the fearful delight of his splendid good fortune.
